opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think continual learning is one of the most important open problems, and I'm not sure anyone has cracked it yet. So I'll describe how I think about it rather than claim we have the answer.

The current paradigm splits things into two phases. You train a model, you freeze it, and you deploy it. Everything the model learns after that point lives in the context window. That works surprisingly well, but it isn't learning in the way humans learn. If you hire someone smart, the first week they're not that useful. By month three they've absorbed a huge amount about how your organization works, and that knowledge is in their head, not in a document they reread every morning. Models today basically reread the document every morning.

So the first thing is being honest that this probably isn't a small tweak. Some people hope that longer context, better retrieval, or memory files will close the gap. Those things help, and we should use them. But I suspect real continual learning needs the weights themselves to change in response to experience, in a way that's stable. The model needs to get better without forgetting, without drifting, and without being easy to poison.

The second thing is that the hard part isn't only the architecture. It's the learning signal. In deployment you don't get clean labels. You get messy, delayed, sometimes adversarial feedback. Reinforcement learning has taught us a lot about learning from sparse rewards, so there's a natural connection there. But doing it online, per user or per organization, at scale, with safety guarantees, is a very different engineering and research problem.

In terms of approach, I'd rather take a few bigger swings than make lots of incremental bets. That means questioning assumptions we've gotten comfortable with, like the strict separation between pretraining, post-training, and inference. It also means building evaluations that actually measure whether a model improves over time on a task. A lot of our benchmarks are static snapshots, and you get what you measure.

And then there's patience. Most of the big shifts in this field looked like they weren't working until suddenly they were. I think continual learning will look like that too. Lots of ideas that seem not to scale, until one does.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. So the honest starting point is that the thing I believe most strongly is that the current paradigm, where you train a model, freeze it, ship it, and then everything it experiences in deployment is basically thrown away, is going to look very strange in retrospect. Every other intelligent system we know of learns from what it does. We've built these incredibly capable things that, in a very literal sense, don't remember yesterday.

So the way we're approaching it is less "let's go find the architecture" and more "let's be honest about which problem is actually the bottleneck." People tend to jump straight to the mechanism, whether it's some new attention variant or a memory module or test-time weight updates, and I think that's often premature. The harder questions are upstream of the architecture.

The first one is: what signal do you even learn from? In pretraining you have this beautiful dense signal, the next token. In RL you have a reward, and we've gotten pretty good at that for things like math and code where you can verify. But in deployment, most of what the model experiences is unlabeled interaction. The user didn't tell you if you were right. They just closed the tab, or they rephrased, or they came back three days later. Extracting a trustworthy learning signal out of that is, in my view, more of a research problem than the architecture is. If you solve the signal problem, I think several architectures would work. If you don't, no architecture saves you.

The second one is stability. The thing that killed continual learning historically is catastrophic forgetting, and it's not a solved problem, it's a problem we've mostly avoided by just not doing online updates. The moment you let the weights move in deployment, you have to answer: how do you prevent the model from drifting in ways you can't see? How do you keep guarantees you cared about at training time? And this is where I think a lot of the architectural work actually matters. You want something where the learning is in some sense compartmentalized, where you can add knowledge or skills without overwriting the core. Whether that looks like a fast-weights system, or retrieval that's tightly integrated with the forward pass, or a hierarchy of parameters updating on different timescales, I genuinely don't know yet, and I'm suspicious of anyone who says they do.

And then the third thing, which is less talked about, is that continual learning is also a systems and product problem. Learning from deployment means the model you serve tomorrow isn't the one you evaluated today. So the eval story has to change completely. You can't just run a benchmark once. You need something closer to continuous monitoring, and you need to be able to roll back. That constrains the design more than people expect.

So practically, what we're doing is starting from the smallest version of the problem that's real. Can a model get measurably better at a narrow class of tasks purely from its own deployment experience, with no human labeling, and without getting worse at anything else? That's a very modest-sounding question. It's surprisingly hard. And I'd rather have a system that passes that test convincingly than a grand architecture that works in a paper and nowhere else.

The thing I try to keep in mind is that the big wins in this field have mostly come from finding a simple, scalable recipe and then just turning the crank. Continual learning doesn't have that recipe yet. The search is for the recipe, not for the architecture. The architecture is what falls out once you know what the recipe is.

r003.rationale: It says architecture choices are premature and the right recipe is unknown; it does not describe using strong architectural priors to guide the search.

astra-6.text:
I think the first thing is to separate two questions: can a system learn from experience, and can it do that reliably while it’s being used? Those are quite different problems.

Deployment gives you a lot of experience, but it doesn’t automatically give you a good learning signal. If somebody corrects the model, is that correction right? Does it apply broadly, or just to that person’s situation? And if you update the system, how do you know you haven’t damaged something it already knew?

So I would approach the architecture search through that learning loop. Give the system a task, let it get feedback, and then test whether that experience helps it handle a new situation. You also have to test whether it retains its earlier capabilities. Otherwise, you can mistake memorizing the latest interaction for progress.

I’d keep an open mind about where that learning happens—in memory, in the model’s weights, or in some combination. The important thing is demonstrating that experience produces improvements that persist and generalize. That’s the behavior I’d want to establish before committing to a particular architecture.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the first thing is to be precise about what we mean by continuous learning. A model can adapt within a conversation, or you can give it a memory, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it’s learning something that will generalize to the next problem.

The question I’m interested in is: can a system encounter something it couldn’t do, learn from that experience, and then reliably do better the next time—without losing capabilities it already had? That’s the behavior we should be testing for, rather than starting with a particular architecture and assuming it’s the answer.

Deployment makes this especially interesting because the feedback is messy. A user correcting the model might be teaching it something broadly useful, or just expressing a personal preference. The system needs to distinguish those cases and decide what to retain.

So I’d approach it as a research loop: build environments where learning is necessary, measure whether improvement transfers and persists, and use those results to guide the architecture. I wouldn’t assume we already know which components need to change.
